blocks.text: Turkish is the language of Anatolia today, but it came from far to the east. Historians and linguists place the early Turkic peoples in Inner Asia, somewhere between the Altai mountains, southern Siberia and Mongolia, more than 5,000 km from Istanbul. Exactly where is still debated.

The name Türk enters written history in the 6th century CE, with a nomadic empire that Chinese sources called Tujue. From what is now Mongolia, it soon stretched west to the Black Sea. The oldest known texts in a Turkic language come from its second khaganate: two stone monuments in the Orkhon valley of Mongolia, raised in 732 and 735 for the prince Kül Tigin and his brother, the ruler Bilge Kagan. They are written in an alphabet that looks like runes, deciphered in 1893 by the Danish linguist Vilhelm Thomsen. The valley is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Over the following centuries, Turkic-speaking groups moved west across the steppe in many waves: herders looking for pasture, soldiers hired by richer neighbours, tribes pushed on by stronger ones. Bulgars, Khazars, Pechenegs and Cumans reached the plains north of the Black Sea. The Oghuz, the branch from which Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen descend, moved toward the Aral Sea. Led by a family called the Seljuks, Oghuz armies took Iran, and in 1055 their ruler Tughril entered Baghdad.

On 26 August 1071, the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert, today *Malazgirt*, north of Lake Van. The battle opened Anatolia to Turkmen groups. A Seljuk sultanate ruled much of the peninsula from Konya until the Mongols defeated it at Kösedağ in 1243; Anatolia then broke up into small principalities, the *beylikler*. One of them, founded around 1300 by Osman, grew into the Ottoman Empire.

Settlement took centuries, and the people already living in Anatolia, Greek, Armenian, Kurdish and many others, did not vanish. Genetic studies find that most people in Turkey today resemble their neighbours far more than they resemble the peoples of Inner Asia: the Turkish language travelled further than the migrants' ancestry did.

blocks.title: A family of languages
blocks.text: Turkic languages are still spoken from the Balkans to eastern Siberia: Azerbaijani, Turkmen, Uzbek, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar, Uyghur and Yakut (Sakha) are all relatives of Turkish.
Here is a short text in the Turkish of this unit:

blocks.tr: Moğolistan İstanbul'dan çok uzak. Ama Moğolistan'da çok eski taşlar var. Bu taşlarda çok eski Türkçe kelimeler var. Bugün Türkiye'den Moğolistan'a turistler gidiyor ve taşlara bakıyor.
blocks.en: Mongolia is very far from Istanbul. But in Mongolia there are very old stones. On these stones there are very old Turkish words. Today tourists go from Turkey to Mongolia and look at the stones.

questions.q: Where were the oldest known texts in a Turkic language found?
options: In the Orkhon valley, in Mongolia
questions.explain: The two Orkhon monuments were raised in 732 and 735.

questions.q: Which battle of 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkmen settlement?
questions.explain: Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert.

questions.q: In the Turkish text, what does *İstanbul'dan* mean?
questions.explain: The ablative `-DAn`: *İstanbul'dan çok uzak*, very far from Istanbul.

sources.title: Orhon inscriptions
sources.note: Found in the Orkhon valley in 1889; monuments of 732 and 735 for Kül and Bilge; deciphered by Vilhelm Thomsen in 1893

sources.title: Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape
sources.note: Inscribed in 2004; includes Turkic memorial sites

sources.title: Turkic peoples
sources.note: The Tujue empire of the 6th century, from Mongolia to the Black Sea; the Sakha of eastern Siberia

sources.title: Seljuq
sources.note: Ruling family of the Oghuz; Tughril in Baghdad, 1055; the Seljuqs of Rum at Konya; Köse Dagh, 1243

sources.title: Battle of Manzikert
sources.note: 26 August 1071, Alp Arslan against Romanus IV Diogenes, followed by the Seljuq conquest of most of Anatolia

sources.title: Turkic migration
sources.note: Proposed homelands; Bulgars, Khazars, Pechenegs, Cumans; the Oghuz after 744

sources.note: Turkic speakers of Anatolia mostly resemble their non-Turkic neighbours; spread mainly through language replacement
